rules.why: The heaviest factor: an IMP incident means the platform failed during a live event.

rules.name: Incident Score range
rules.why: Value 0 to 8 maps linearly onto the cap. Two fresh critical incidents already come to 10, past the cap.

rules.name: Open Bug Weight cap
rules.why: What is broken right now. No decay by design: it falls the moment a bug closes, so the factor rewards fixing things.

rules.drives: Quality penalty

rules.name: Open Bug Weight range
rules.why: Weighted 10 is roughly three Urgent bugs plus a High.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: Client Bug Score cap
rules.why: Two years of accumulated bug pain, decayed. An open bug counts in both this and Open Bug Weight, deliberately.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Quality penalty

rules.name: Client Bug Score range
rules.why: 40 is roughly thirteen fresh Urgent bugs, or more already part-decayed.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Quality penalty

rules.name: Total quality penalty cap
rules.why: Headroom is deliberate: if quality could consume the whole 0-10 scale, the relationship factors would stop mattering exactly on the accounts where they are most interesting.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Penalty chart axis, at-cap KPI, health factor bars

rules.name: At-the-cap threshold
rules.why: An arbitrary threshold, chosen to catch rounding just short of the cap. Worth arguing about.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard
rules.drives: The "at the cap" KPI tile

rules.name: Formula must be linear, not linear (bounded)
rules.value: linear
rules.why: With "bounded", a value past the top of the range scores no penalty at all — so the worst accounts, the ones furthest past the cap, come out clean. Check this whenever a factor is edited in Planhat.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: Planhat bug weights
rules.value: Urgent 3, High 2, Medium 1, Low 0; no priority counts as Medium (1)
rules.why: Low weighs zero, so a client whose open bugs are all Low shows 0 — correct, but it looks broken next to a Jira list. An untriaged ticket must never score better than a triaged one, hence Medium for no-priority.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: Renewal anchor discount
rules.value: Anything raised before the client's most recent Won deal counts at 25%
rules.why: A renewal renews trust; it does not erase history.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: Decay half-life
rules.value: 180 days, over a 24-month window — Incident Score and Client Bug Score only
rules.why: Open Client Bug Weight has NO decay. Assuming the decay governs all three factors is the easiest mistake to make.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: The join key
rules.value: Pipedrive Company ID — stored in Planhat as the Company externalId field
rules.why: The ONLY key anything joins on. Names are never joined: Jira labels, Planhat names and the contract sheet all spell the same client differently, and matching on text is how clients silently vanish.
rules.source: Susan's Customer & Event workbook, Overview tab

rules.name: Which client gets a bug
rules.value:
1. If EVERY Reported-by value is INTERNAL, discard — not a client experience.
2. If any label has an override mapping, use only those companies.
3. Otherwise use Planhat's own companyIds on the Issue.
4. Otherwise map each label through the Reported-by Label Dictionary to a Pipedrive company id.
rules.why: The signal is "Reported by", not "Affected clients", because Reported by records who actually hit the problem. Step 3 is stronger than it looks: a bug with NO Reported-by value still counts when the connector linked it to a company.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: A ticket with several clients
rules.value: Counts in full against every one of them
rules.why: One platform bug penalises ten accounts identically for one root cause. If several unrelated accounts move together, check this first.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: Partner files, customer owns
rules.value: Mapped to the customer, not the party who filed
rules.why: Health belongs to the company whose event is affected.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: Which client gets an incident
rules.value: Override labels first, then the Pipedrive Company ID field, then the plain dictionary
rules.why: Deliberately different from the bug order. Automation for Jira stamps the Pipedrive Company ID within seconds of creation, so this resolves cleanly.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: Which client gets a story
rules.value:
1. A story counts for a client ONLY if it carries that client's label in Jira. 61 of 650 do.
2. Labels join through the same Pipedrive dictionary the bug side uses.
3. INTERNAL-labelled and unlabelled stories become the platform band — never attributed to a client.
rules.why: Much weaker than the bug side, and the asymmetry is the point: it is why investment and liability are never netted (il-not-commensurable) and why the Investment column is a question to ask, not an answer.
rules.source: Delivery Timeline

rules.name: Reported vs affected
rules.value: The dashboard shows both; only the Reported-by side feeds the Health Score
rules.why: The operating question is "what will the client hit", but the score only sees who reported it. The Clients tab toggle switches between the two views.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard

rules.name: Jira EP bug feed
rules.value:
project = EP AND issuetype = Bug AND statusCategory != Done
AND (cf[10145] != "INTERNAL" OR cf[12190] is not EMPTY)
rules.why: The JQL printed on the old Sources tab returns 324, not 84 — it does not encode the INTERNAL discard. This corrected form returns 76; JQL CANNOT express the real rule, because it drops a ticket if ANY value is INTERNAL while the rule drops it only if EVERY value is. The discard must happen in extraction.
rules.source: Measured live 18 Sep 2026

rules.name: Jira IMP incident feed
rules.value:
project = IMP AND created >= -180d
AND reporter != "System"
AND summary !~ "Grafana"
AND summary !~ "TEST"
AND summary !~ "Uptime"
rules.why: Returns 42 of 55. Dropping the non-production ticket, the post-snapshot one and an App Store setting gives the dashboard's 39. Nothing the dashboard kept is dropped by this rule, which is what makes it trustworthy.
rules.source: Reconstructed 18 Sep 2026 by diffing all 55 against the dashboard's 39

rules.name: What is excluded from IMP
rules.value:
Grafana / monitoring alerts (8) — reporter = System, summaries start [Grafana]: [FIRING:1]
Explicit test tickets (3)
Uptime-monitoring noise raised by humans (2)
Non-production environments (1) — alpha2 is not production
Raised after the snapshot (1)
Not a production service disruption (1)
rules.why: Incidents are "ongoing problems on production that affect our clients". Everything excluded fails that test. reporter = System alone accounts for half.
rules.source: Incident Management Process, Engineering space

rules.name: Severity and SLA targets
rules.value:
SEV0 Critical (Urgent): respond <30 min, resolve 2-4 h, Post Mortem in 3 days
SEV1 High: respond <1 h, resolve 4-8 h, Post Mortem in 7 days
SEV2 Medium: respond 8 h, resolve 8-24 h, Post Mortem optional
SEV3 Low: respond next business day, resolve 2-3 business days
rules.why: Severity IS the ticket priority. These targets make MTTA/MTTR/SLA computable from Jira rather than typed in by hand.
rules.source: Incident Management Process

rules.name: Computing MTTA and MTTR
rules.value:
MTTA = created until customfield_12074 "Incident manager" is first set (changelog)
MTTR = created until the LAST transition into a done status (changelog)
resolutiondate and resolution are null on every IMP ticket — the standard field is useless here
rules.why: Take the LAST done transition: IMP-321 went Testing to Done to Testing to Done, and using the first understates MTTR by a day.
rules.source: Proven on IMP-321, 18 Sep 2026

rules.name: Pre-2026 column
rules.value: Everything raised before 2026-01 collapses into one leading column
rules.why: 29 of the 84 open bugs predate January, the oldest from September 2023. Without that column a third of the backlog is invisible, which flatters the picture considerably.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard

rules.name: Bugs bucket by raised date
rules.value: The month the bug was created — not closed
rules.why: Every bug in the set is currently OPEN, so the lower strip reads "raised in this month and still open today". It is not a throughput measure. That makes leftward drift the signal: bars far left are the ageing backlog.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard

rules.name: Bar scaling
rules.value: Scaled against the busiest VISIBLE cell, so the grid re-scales as filters change
rules.why: Widths are comparable within one view and never across two.

rules.name: Planhat returns HTTP 200 for a field that does not exist
rules.value: Renaming any of the four nightly-written fields silently freezes every company on yesterday's value
rules.why: No error is raised anywhere. Rename in the workflow and the digest QUALITY array in the same sitting, or create the new field, write both for a week, then retire the old.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: Closure detected from status name, not statusCategory
rules.value: A new "closed" status matching no known substring keeps its bugs counted as open
rules.why: The Planhat Issue model does not expose statusCategory, so the job matches substrings. Check every new status against that list.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: Caps and weights live in three places
rules.value:
Planhat Health Score Profile — what actually moves the score
n8n Compute Health Factors node in jpuksPy0UTJJHO6D — mirrored, so the breakdown text matches
n8n Compute Digest node in 3hyLMUGOn21IctQt — the QUALITY array for the weekly email
rules.why: Change one without the others and the explanations start contradicting the score.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: IMP tickets close without a resolution
rules.value: resolutiondate and resolution are null on every IMP ticket, including Done ones
rules.why: Any tool reading the standard field gets nothing. Timing must come from the changelog.
rules.source: Measured 18 Sep 2026

rules.name: Not every live problem becomes a ticket
rules.value: The Health Score only sees what is in IMP
rules.why: The lead-scanning issue behind the Tampere invoice dispute was raised as IMP-317 only after the fact. A client can have a bad quarter the model never registers.
rules.source: OPKL — Bug and Incident Factors guide, reviewed 14 Sep 2026

rules.name: Informa (82918) is a group parent, not a customer
rules.value: Counted as a client today: Tier 4, health 9, no bugs, no delivery
rules.why: The workbook says so explicitly and excludes it. Its two real subsidiaries are separate, correct records. Until decided, "49 active clients" should read 48.
rules.source: Susan's Customer & Event workbook, Overview tab

rules.name: Incidents with no client
rules.value: 8 of 39 carry no client at all
rules.why: They cannot appear in any client-level view, including the timeline.
rules.source: Jira IMP

rules.name: Only 61 of 650 stories carry a client label
rules.value: 109 are INTERNAL, 483 unlabelled
rules.why: The investment axis is thin by construction (il-denominators). The platform band keeps the unattributed work visible without inventing attribution.
rules.source: Delivery Timeline

rules.name: K5 GmbH is no longer Phase = Active
rules.value: In Jira and the contract sheet, but no tier, health or computed factors
rules.why: Carried anyway so its bugs are not silently lost.
rules.source: Planhat

rules.name: Story summaries are AI-written
rules.value: 92 of 650 flagged low confidence and marked as such wherever they appear
rules.why: Written from the Jira description and any linked spec, never invented. Treat a low-confidence summary as a pointer to the ticket, not a statement of fact.
rules.source: Delivery Timeline

rules.name: This model supersedes the old story scoring
rules.value: Replaces value-framework v3 (Tier x Reach x max(Impact) x Confidence, 0-200) and impact-lenses v1 (six lenses with EXP as a hardcoded catch-all). The Delivery tab on this page still shows the old model: lens, business value High/Medium/Low, revenue goal and a v score. None of it converts. Historical scores are regenerated, never mapped.
rules.why: Rebuilding the Delivery tab on this model needs twelve fields that the inherited story dataset does not carry. Until that pull exists, the Delivery tab and this group describe different systems.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Scope
rules.value: project = EP AND issuetype = Story AND created >= "2026-01-01" AND status != Rejected
rules.why: Nothing else is filtered. Both delivered and in-flight work enters the model and the output labels which is which. Measured 1,201 stories on 20 Sep 2026, against the 650 this page inherited from the Delivery Timeline.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: The unit is the story
rules.value: One story, one record. Epic aggregation is gone.
rules.why: The old model summed member story values into an epic total, so twenty small stories outranked three important ones and bubble size rewarded volume as much as worth.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Sub-tasks are never records
rules.value: Read only to roll their tracked time up to the parent story
rules.why: Keeps the story as the single unit while still capturing effort the OTE process pushes down a level.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: What an epic is allowed to do
rules.value: Carried as epic_key and epic_name from the Jira parent field, with customfield_10014 as fallback. It groups: totalling effort across an initiative, pulling siblings into a detail view, and a coherence check when one epic scatters across four themes. It never sizes a point, never enters a score and is never drawn as a boundary. Effort may sum across an epic. Value may not.
rules.why: Value is not additive, and summing it is precisely the v3 failure. A story with no epic is simply ungrouped, so the old hidden Unclassified bucket cannot recur.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Never read epic status or epic effort
rules.value: Both are unusable at EP
rules.why: EP-49994 sits at Ready to start while its own child EP-53978 is Done and resolved. Epic OTE is a temporary buffer meant to be reduced as stories are created, and that reduction is inconsistent, so it is a stale placeholder of unknown provenance.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: An epic name may reveal a client the story does not
rules.value: Surface as a review prompt, never resolve a tier from it
rules.why: An epic title is far too loose to score from. Checked on EP-53978: its epic is titled IMEX GDPR Requirements, and the story itself carries Reported By tokens DLG and FBF, so the epic title would have pointed at a third client entirely.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Seconds per day
rules.why: An 8 hour day and a 5 day week, confirmed by 230400 seconds rendering as 1w 3d on EP-53978. It belongs in config, not inline, because changing the Jira setting would silently move every number in the model.
rules.source: Estimation process based on OTE

rules.name: ote_days
rules.value: timeoriginalestimate / 28800
rules.why: Story level only. The OTE process defines a story OTE as the entire cross-functional effort: design, product, development, code review, bug fixing, release and QA.
rules.source: Estimation process based on OTE

rules.name: spent_days
rules.value: aggregatetimespent / 28800
rules.why: Story and its sub-tasks, because the tracked time for that same cross-functional effort is logged across the sub-tasks. This is what the Jira UI shows with Include subtasks ticked. On EP-53978 the 25 children sum to 131,400 seconds, exactly 765,000 minus 633,600.
rules.source: Estimation process based on OTE

rules.name: rte_days
rules.value: ote_days - spent_days
rules.why: Computed, never read. Jira's own Remaining Estimate floors at zero and is manually maintained: EP-53978 reads 0 remaining while its real RTE is 8 - 26.6 = -18.6 days. The negative is the interesting number and Jira will never supply it.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Never read aggregatetimeoriginalestimate
rules.value: It sums the story OTE with its sub-tasks' OTEs
rules.why: Where a team decomposes but leaves the story OTE in place, the same work is counted twice. Reading story level removes the exposure outright. Measured 20 Sep 2026: about 12 of the 939 unestimated stories have an estimate on sub-tasks instead, so the exposure is structural rather than common.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Rejected sub-tasks still count
rules.value: Their logged time counts
rules.why: The hours were genuinely spent whether or not the sub-task was later abandoned. Rejected is a scope exclusion at story level only. Three of EP-53978's children sit at Rejected.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: The missing-OTE placeholder
rules.value: Median ote_days of completed stories in the same theme. If a theme has too few completed stories, fall back to the median across all completed stories and say so on the report. The story sets ote_estimated = true, renders hollow or dashed, and is excluded from every estimate-versus-actual statistic.
rules.why: Comparing a real actual against an invented estimate would corrupt the predictability number, which is the one thing the OTE process exists to produce. Measured 20 Sep 2026: 939 of 1,201 stories in scope carry no OTE, so this rule governs 78 percent of the population, not the margin.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: in_flight
rules.value: True when the live status is not in the done set
rules.why: An in-flight story displays OTE as a baseline bar, tracked as the filled portion and RTE as a tail, red when negative. In-flight effort counts toward total spend because the days are gone; it does not count toward cost of delivered value. Both figures are reported separately and labelled.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Two things the effort number is not
rules.value: It is not elapsed time: EP-53978's 26.6 days were logged by several people across several weeks, so axes must say person-days or the chart reads as a timeline. It is not total engineering capacity: the OTE process routes meetings and rituals to a separate Others ticket per team, so any percentage claim reads "of tracked story effort", never "of engineering".
rules.why: Both mistakes are easy to make from the same number. Axes must say person-days or the chart reads as a timeline, and any percentage claim reads "of tracked story effort", never "of engineering".
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Unresolved: the 6 hour man-day
rules.value: The OTE process defines a man-day as 6 hours for Rough Estimation while Jira converts at 8
rules.why: EP-53978 is 8 Jira-days or 10.7 man-days. It does not affect the model, which is internally consistent in Jira days, but it moves any money figure by a third.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: The five classes
rules.value: Contracted: a client is owed this under contract, scores on the tier ladder. Client-driven: a client asked and we chose to build, tier ladder. Growth bet: nobody asked, built to win or expand business, growth ladder. Platform investment: nobody asked, built to improve the platform, investment ladder. Necessity: we had no real choice, no value score at all.
rules.why: The class decides which ladder computes a story's value and whether it gets one. Work we chose is scored separately from work we had no choice about.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Necessity wins every tie
rules.value: A story that is arguably both a client request and a compliance obligation is a necessity
rules.why: We would have built it either way, so attributing its value to a client overstates what that relationship earned us.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: The five necessity reasons
rules.value: Compliance, Security, Breakage, Vendor deprecation, Scale ceiling
rules.why: They exist so the non-discretionary total can be broken down rather than being one opaque number. Necessity stories plot at effort only and produce the headline: N person-days of 2026 went to work we had no choice about.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Contracted against Client-driven
rules.value: Worth two points on the ladder, and there is no field in Jira for it
rules.why: Reported By establishes that a client was involved, never that we were obliged. The LLM proposes it from the ticket text and it is corrected by hand where wrong.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Value range
rules.value: Integer 2 to 10, or absent for a Necessity
rules.why: Every rung is reachable, which was not true of the old model. There is no multiplication anywhere: each class picks one ladder, one rung and at most one modifier. Multiplying correlated factors compounds their error; a ladder does not.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Commercial ladder, Contracted and Client-driven
rules.value: Contracted: Tier 1 = 10, Tier 2 = 8, Tier 3 = 6, Tier 4 = 4. Client-driven: Tier 1 = 8, Tier 2 = 6, Tier 3 or 4 = 4.
rules.why: Being owed something is worth one tier's worth of value over having been asked for it, so a Tier 1 client asking nicely and a Tier 2 client holding a contract both land on 8.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Growth ladder, Growth bet
rules.value: 8 opens a market or product line we cannot currently sell into; 4 speculative feature, built hoping it lands
rules.why: Two rungs, because ranking speculation more finely would be false precision. The expected value Commercial attaches carries the real signal.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Investment ladder, Platform investment
rules.value: 10 unlocks revenue we currently cannot sell. 8 removes a scale or risk ceiling that is blocking growth. 6 makes many future features cheaper or faster to build. 4 cuts run cost or manual labour. 2 local cleanup, one team benefits.
rules.why: A platform investment can reach 10, which the old model made impossible for anything client-adjacent.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: The spread modifier
rules.value: +2 if the work generalises to every client rather than staying bespoke to the requester, capped at 10, Contracted and Client-driven only
rules.why: The single most important distinction the old model could not express: building a feature for one client and building the same feature into the product are different acts with different returns. It does not apply to the other three classes, which are platform-wide by definition or carry no score.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Resolving Reported By to a tier
rules.value: customfield_10145 is split on comma. INTERNAL and Not Clearly Specified are discarded. Multiple clients resolve to the highest tier, not a sum and not an average. No client token is not a tier question: the story is a Growth bet, Platform investment or Necessity, none of which use the tier ladder. An unrecognised token becomes Tier 4 plus a data quality entry. K5 GmbH - Future Retail is Tier 4, carried without a tier so its stories still score.
rules.why: The old model defaulted an unknown client to Enterprise/Large, its second-highest weight, which quietly inflated everything it touched.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: A bare Informa token stops the run
rules.value: The only data quality finding that halts anything
rules.why: It matches the group parent record, which is not a customer, while its subsidiaries are Tier 1. Silently resolving it to Tier 4 would score Tier 1 work at the bottom of the ladder.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Alias map
rules.value: Regent Exhibitions Limited -> IMEX (legal entity), Tier 1. Cosmoprof -> BolognaFiere, Tier 2. FBF and FrankfurterBuchmesse -> Frankfurter Buchmesse GmbH, Tier 1. Informa-Fashion and Informa-MRO -> an Informa subsidiary, Tier 1 either way. Informa bare -> hard error.
rules.why: The Jira tokens and the client list do not use the same names. The map is expected to grow, and every unmatched token lands on the report, so it grows by evidence rather than guesswork.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Tier is the only client attribute that scores
rules.value: Health is carried for reporting and never enters a score; Won TCV is no longer carried on this dashboard at all
rules.why: Health moves continuously and would make last quarter's chart unreproducible. Revenue was removed from this dashboard on 21 Sep 2026, so tier is the only commercial signal left on the page.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Retention-critical
rules.value: Tier 1 or 2 and health 3 or below, display only
rules.why: On the current list that is Frankfurter Buchmesse (0), HINTE (0), DLG (1), DWTC (2) and ANWR (3). Marking those stories visibly is more useful than burying health inside a weight.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: The eight structural themes
rules.value: Registration & Ticketing, Exhibitor & Sponsor, Lead Intelligence, Networking & Meetings, Content & Sessions, Data Reporting & Integrations, Admin & Organiser Tools, Platform & Infrastructure.
rules.why: Themes say where in the platform the work landed, not what it was worth, because value has its own axis now. Eight is roughly the ceiling for a legible colour legend. Lead Intelligence stands alone because it is a distinct product surface with its own screens and its own buyer.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: ux is a boolean, not a theme
rules.value: The story keeps the theme of the module it changed, and ux = true shades the point. The same pattern extends later to accessibility or performance without touching the theme list.
rules.why: UX is a property of work done somewhere else in the product, not a place in it. As a theme it would give every story that touched a screen two valid homes. The current system shows the failure mode: EXP is hardcoded True as the final catch-all, which is why Experience absorbs everything that falls through.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: No catch-all and no default theme
rules.value: A story the LLM cannot theme returns unsure and goes to the review queue
rules.why: An unthemed story is a question for a human, not a silent assignment to whichever bucket happens to be last in the list.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: The six LLM-proposed fields
rules.value: class, necessity_reason, investment_level, spread, theme, ux
rules.why: Each comes back with a one-line reason and a certainty. The ladders are given verbatim as the rubric: the LLM is asked which rung's test the story meets, never to judge value, so judgement stays on classification where it is reliable.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Override always wins
rules.value: Human corrections live in a separate file keyed by story. The pipeline reads it and never writes it. A re-run over a story with an override does not call the LLM for that field at all, and the override is permanent until a human removes it.
rules.why: This is what makes the ability to change survive the second build. If the LLM re-decides every field on every run, every correction evaporates the next time someone runs the pipeline, and people stop correcting.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Provenance is reported
rules.value: llm = proposed and never reviewed, confirmed = a human agreed, override = a human corrected
rules.why: If 90 percent of the map is llm, the map is a first draft. That is fine as long as it says so.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Unsure is a valid answer
rules.value: The LLM may return unsure on any field rather than being forced to pick
rules.why: A forced guess is indistinguishable from a confident answer once it is written down, which is worse than an admitted gap.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: What the prompt does not see
rules.value: Effort, tier and any previously computed value are withheld
rules.why: A 26-day story must not look more strategic to the model simply because it was expensive.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Following links out of a description
rules.value: Three link forms must be extracted from the ADF description: inline links carrying an href mark, smart links as inlineCard or blockCard nodes with the URL often inside an xpis blob, and bare URLs in plain text. Confluence and Jira are fetched through the Atlassian connector, external links where a connector exists and recorded unreachable where none does. Depth 1 only, and fetched pages are cached by URL for the run.
rules.why: A large share of EP stories carry a stub description with the real specification in a linked page, so classifying from the stub means classifying from a title. Each story records source_refs, so any classification can be audited back to its evidence. A stub whose links are all unreachable returns unsure on every field rather than being guessed from the summary line.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Data quality findings and their owners
rules.value: OTE missing -> Engineering, placeholder used and excluded from estimate stats. Time tracked zero on a completed story -> Engineering, excluded from the scatter. Actual exceeds the 2-week story cap -> Engineering, plots and is flagged for splitting. Reported By token unrecognised -> TAM, Tier 4 applied. Bare Informa token -> TAM, run stops. Contracted with no contract_value -> Commercial, plots normally. Growth bet with no expected value -> Commercial, plots normally. LLM returned unsure -> Product, review queue. Stub description with unreachable links -> Engineering, review queue.
rules.why: Only one finding halts the run. Everything else degrades visibly and keeps going, because a chart that refuses to render until the data is perfect never renders. The report is diffed between runs: a growing list means the underlying discipline is slipping.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Two counts at the top of every run
rules.value: Stories with real effort data as a percentage, and fields still at llm provenance as a percentage
rules.why: They set how much weight the output can bear. Measured 20 Sep 2026 the first is 16 percent: 193 of 1,201 stories carry both an estimate and logged time.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Validation gates, any failure blocks the output
rules.value: Correctness: every story has exactly one class; every non-Necessity story has a value between 2 and 10; every Necessity story has no value and one reason; no story has both an override and a fresh LLM proposal on the same field; value recomputes identically from its stored inputs; every Reported By token resolved or is on the report. Arithmetic: rte_days == ote_days - spent_days for every story; effort roll-ups sum to the story-level total; no effort double-counted between a story and its sub-tasks. Presentation: no overlapping points or labels; zero em dashes and en dashes anywhere in the output; the SVG parses as XML; the in-flight count on the chart matches the ledger.
rules.why: Since value is a pure function of class, tier, investment_level and spread, the recompute check is cheap and catches almost everything worth catching. Note that this page does not currently meet the em dash rule, which applies to the model's own output.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: A re-run over unchanged inputs must be byte-identical
rules.value: Any drift means something non-deterministic crept in
rules.why: For a chart people make decisions from that is a defect regardless of whether the numbers look plausible.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: What the old model got wrong
rules.value: Tier x Reach x max(Impact) x Confidence: four factors, two nearly constant, compounding error. Confidence multiplier: Low -> 0.5 penalised ticket-writing quality, not business reality. Measured confidence: 1.0 was never auto-assignable, so the 250 ceiling was fiction. Five-level Reach: levels 1 and 2 were unreachable. max(Impact) over 5 categories: a second impact category added nothing. Client-check-first tier rule: capped client work at 7. Unmapped client -> Enterprise/Large. Epic aggregation by sum. CAP = 9. Hidden Unclassified bucket. Circle packing. Hardcoded EXP = True catch-all. Six-level chip precedence. shipped counting. Business Value High/Med/Low running parallel to the score.
rules.why: The triple penalty is the one to remember: thin documentation cost 0.5 on confidence, dropped tier to 2 through a Not Clearly Specified beneficiary, and forced Cost Reduction at 3 with no impact signal. A badly written but genuinely important story came out small. All three inputs are gone, so documentation quality now affects one thing only: whether the LLM can classify the story.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Effort coverage, measured 20 Sep 2026
rules.value: Of 1,201 stories in scope: 262 carry a story-level estimate (21.8 percent), 939 do not (78.2 percent), 583 have logged time (48.5 percent), 193 have both (16.1 percent), 574 are Done (47.8 percent) and 176 are Done with an estimate (14.7 percent). About 12 of the 939 have an estimate on sub-tasks instead.
rules.why: Answers the first item on the spec's confirm-before-first-run list. Decomposition is a rounding error; the 939 are genuinely unestimated. So the placeholder rule governs four stories in five, every per-story effort number is a statement about 262 stories, and every estimate-versus-actual number a statement about 193.
rules.source: Live Jira through the connector, 20 Sep 2026

rules.name: JQL cannot filter on aggregate time fields
rules.value: aggregateTimeOriginalEstimate is not EMPTY is accepted and silently ignored, returning 0
rules.why: It returned 0 against issues whose value had already been read directly, so the clause is not evaluated. Anyone sizing decomposition from JQL alone gets a confidently wrong answer. Read the field per issue instead.
rules.source: Live Jira through the connector, 20 Sep 2026

rules.name: Parked: the money layer
rules.value: Needs a blended day rate and a decision on whether a day is 6 or 8 hours
rules.why: Once settled it unlocks non-discretionary spend in pounds, cost-to-serve per client against Won TCV, and spend cross-referenced against health for the five retention-critical accounts. Every story already carries days, class and tier, so the layer bolts on without touching anything.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Still to confirm
rules.value: Informa-Fashion and Informa-MRO: both Tier 1 either way so scoring is unaffected, but cost-to-serve needs them resolved to Markets UK or North America. CEO list reconciliation: five items were unresolved against the working list, namely whether it is four tiers or five, DWTC appearing at two tiers, Connect's absence, four unfamiliar names, and two clients dropped without a churn status.
rules.why: The decomposition count, the third item on the original list, is now measured and recorded above. The spec uses the working list throughout.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Deliberately not modelled
rules.value: Health as a score input, carried as the retention-critical flag instead. Tier granularity: splitting Tier 1 is a live option, but not before seeing a run. Effort banding: raw days on a continuous axis, bands only if the scatter proves hard to read.
rules.why: Health moves monthly and would make a prior quarter's chart unreproducible. Tier 1 spans 520k to 3.58m and Tier 4 spans 9k to 44k, so a 2.5x score spread already covers a 400x revenue spread.
rules.source: Story Value & Effort Model v1 spec, 19 Sep 2026

rules.name: Which client gets a story
rules.value: A story attaches to a client through the client tokens in its Jira Reported by field (customfield_10145, the dataset's tags), resolved to Pipedrive company ids in the pds field; INTERNAL marks it internal and names nobody. A story carrying two client tokens appears in both client rows and is counted once in each, so the band totals exceed the story count where they overlap. A story naming no client is platform work and appears in the platform band under the team that built it, never against a client.
rules.why: Checked 24 Sep 2026: all 61 inherited tagged stories match their Reported by values and none matches its Jira labels, so the earlier wording (labels) described the wrong field. Deliberately different from the bug rule: a story has no Pipedrive stamp. 70 of 684 stories name a client, so the client rows are thin by construction.
rules.source: Delivery Timeline dataset + live Jira

rules.name: Which client gets a bug
rules.value: Reported By and Affected Clients, resolved to Pipedrive ids, per the Attribution group
rules.why: Bugs attach to clients, not to stories. This dataset holds no link between a bug and the story that caused it: the Jira issue-link and sub-task relationships that would carry it were never pulled. Any claim about defects a feature generated needs that pull first and cannot be made from this page.
rules.source: Jira EP

rules.name: No bug is attached to a story here
rules.value: The join does not exist in this dataset
rules.why: Worth stating plainly so nobody reads the delivery and bug strips in one cell as cause and effect. They are two independent attributions to the same client in the same month, not a story and its defects. The spec's own worked example shows the shape it would take: EP-53978 carries 16 Defect sub-tasks, which live on the story, not in the client bug list.
rules.source: Delivery Timeline dataset + live Jira

rules.name: Time to deliver a story
rules.value: resolutiondate - created, in whole calendar days
rules.why: Elapsed calendar days, not person-days and not effort. It counts weekends, holidays and every day a ticket sat untouched. The effort figure is a different measure entirely and lives in the story model group.
rules.source: Live Jira through the connector, 20 Sep 2026

rules.name: Delivery time is measurable on 269 of 650
rules.value: Median 77 days, first quartile 43, third quartile 95, longest 235 (EP-48506). By theme the median runs Integrations 95, Cost 77, Revenue 77, AI 76, Experience 64, Data 50. By team it runs Integration 95, Visitor 77, Organizer 75, Exhibitor 68, Mobile 61, Data Science 43, Staff 31.
rules.why: The other 381 stories have no resolution date, so their delivery time is unknown rather than zero. Every median on this page is computed over the measurable subset only and says so where it is shown.
rules.source: Live Jira through the connector, 20 Sep 2026

rules.name: Which month a story is placed in
rules.value: The month of resolutiondate where Jira has one. Where it does not, the month the story was raised.
rules.why: Measured on all 650: where a resolution date exists the inherited month matches it 258 times out of 269, and the 11 exceptions all resolved between 16 and 18 Sep, after the dataset snapshot. Where no resolution date exists the inherited month equals the created month 381 times out of 381, with no exceptions. So the fallback is certain, and 59 percent of this timeline is placed by when work started rather than when it landed. Read a month column as "raised or delivered", never as delivered alone.
rules.source: Live Jira through the connector, 20 Sep 2026

rules.name: Eleven stories have moved since the snapshot
rules.why: All eleven read In Progress in the 16 Sep dataset and Done in Jira on 20 Sep. The story analysis shows both, marking the snapshot value where the two disagree, rather than silently preferring one.
rules.source: Live Jira through the connector, 20 Sep 2026

rules.name: Over half of Done stories carry no resolution date
rules.value: 303 of the 571 stories Jira calls Done have resolutiondate null
rules.why: The same defect already recorded for IMP incidents, now confirmed on EP stories. Any tool that measures cycle time from resolutiondate silently drops more than half the completed work. Fixing it at source needs a resolution set on close; until then the changelog is the only complete route.
rules.source: Live Jira through the connector, 20 Sep 2026

rules.name: The Delivery tab opens on the timeline
rules.value: Timeline is the default view; the story list is behind the View toggle
rules.why: A list of 650 stories answers "what did we build" and nothing else. The grid answers when, for whom, and at what rate, which is what the tab is read for.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard

rules.name: How the rows are banded
rules.value: Tier 1, Tier 2, Tier 3, Tier 4, then no tier in Planhat, then platform work. Clients sit inside their tier band, ordered by story count descending then by name. Each band opens with a total row.
rules.why: The same banding as the main Timeline tab, so the two grids read alike and a client sits in the same place on both.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard

rules.name: The platform band is split by product area, or by team with a switch
rules.value: One row per product area (the product catalogue's top level: rule dl-product-area), not one row for all platform stories. The Platform rows switch on the Delivery tab turns the band back to one row per team; the viewer's choice is remembered in their own browser only. The Product area filter narrows every view to one area or one product within it.
rules.why: Platform work is about 90 percent of the dataset. A single row would make the largest part of the year unreadable. Product area answers what the work was for; team, the grouping this band used before 25 Sep 2026, answers who built it, so both stay one click apart.
rules.source: Ajay, 24 Sep 2026: "instead of team level the work must be classified into product areas the top most heirarchy and that must be the main filter for this and you can switch to team level by a toggle."

rules.name: Every story has one product and one product area, taken from the product knowledge base's catalogue
rules.value: Product areas and products are the catalogue in the product knowledge base (MASTER Product Ecosystem Map §3-§4): Provisioning & Platform Core, Acquisition & Commerce, Identity & Community, Engagement & Matchmaking, Exhibitor & Sponsor, Onsite, Insight, and Cross-cutting (the knowledge base's own Unassigned bucket). Each story gets one product by the first rule that decides: its Jira component where the component names a product (§12 table), unless the story text clearly shows the work belongs to another product or to none; then its epic's name; then its summary and what/why/outcome text matched to a product's documented features; otherwise Cross-cutting. The Admin Interface component names a surface, not a product. Each record keeps the rule used, the evidence, the feature line cited and a confidence. Classified 25 Sep 2026 for all 1,196 cached stories (data/stories/pa, SPEC v2); the 684 page stories carry it. The story's older AI product tag is kept alongside, unchanged.
rules.why: Team says who built the work; the owner asked for what it was for, at the top level of the product hierarchy. Borrowing the knowledge base's catalogue and its own assignment rule means the areas are not invented here and match the product documentation. Components alone put about 75 stories in the wrong area (mostly Admin Interface on other products' settings, and team chores), so the owner chose on 25 Sep 2026 that clear story content overrides the component.
rules.source: product-intelligence-graph-architect knowledge base, master-extraction.md §3, §4, §12 (line 483). Owner decisions: Ajay, 24 and 25 Sep 2026.

rules.name: Bar widths scale to the busiest visible cell
rules.value: Each cell bar is its story count over the maximum count in view, floored at 12 percent so a single story stays visible
rules.why: The grid re-scales as filters change, so bar length compares cells within one view and never across two different filters. Band total rows scale against their own band maximum, not the grid maximum.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard

rules.name: Every story carries its full analysis
rules.value: Status, raised date, resolved date, time to deliver, placement month and its basis, theme, product area, team, epic, business value, revenue goal, impact categories, confidence, client labels, then the problem, why it was done and what changed.
rules.why: Collapsed until clicked, so a cell holding 40 stories stays readable. Shown identically in the Delivery timeline, the main Timeline and the client record, so one story reads the same everywhere. A low-confidence summary is marked wherever it appears: it was written from the Jira description and any linked spec, so treat it as a pointer to the ticket rather than a statement of fact.
rules.source: Delivery Timeline dataset + live Jira

rules.name: Stories sit under the epic Jira gives them, and an epic's progress is read from its stories
rules.value: Epic = the story's Jira parent where that parent is an Epic (hierarchy level 1), read on each story pull; the epic may sit in another project (EI, HV). EP epics have no parent, so the hierarchy is two levels: story, then epic. The Epics view on the Delivery tab groups the ledger's stories by that epic and counts shipped and in progress from the stories themselves. The epic's own Jira status is shown only as Jira's, and flagged where it disagrees with its stories. A story with no parent is listed under No epic, never guessed from its title.
rules.why: The dataset carried an epic name and no key, so nothing could be grouped or opened, and 13 of the names had gone stale by 24 Sep as stories moved epics. Epic status is not read as progress because it does not track its children at EP (sv-epic-status).
rules.source: Ajay, 24 Sep 2026: "we are missing story - epic hierarchy please add that so we can see that". Checked live: 0 of 365 EP epics has a parent.

rules.name: The page carries stories that have shipped or started; stories not yet started stay in the cache
rules.value: Page stories = the 650 inherited from the Delivery Timeline (16 Sep 2026) plus every other in-scope 2026 story whose Jira status category is In Progress or Done at the story pull, 34 on 24 Sep 2026 (27 in progress, 7 shipped), marked added. Stories in To Do (Open, Ready to start: 512 on 24 Sep) are held in data/stories/cache with their text and epic but are not on the page, because investment counts shipped or in-progress work only (il-investment-unit).
rules.why: Adding the backlog would have counted planned work as delivery and moved clients across the quadrant. The owner chose, 24 Sep 2026, to add only the started and shipped stories.
rules.source: Ajay, 24 Sep 2026.

rules.name: Where event dates come from
rules.value: project = OP AND issuetype = 10080  /* Delivery of Events & Communities */
rules.why: Live and re-pullable, unlike the monthly workbook export the dashboard used before. 719 tickets exist in total; this page carries the 275 ending on or after 1 Jan 2026, which is the window the delivery grid covers plus everything still to come.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Which field is which date
rules.value: customfield_10015 is the event START date. duedate is the event END date, the last day. Both are present on all 275 events pulled, with no gaps.
rules.why: Verified against the workbook on multi-day events: OP-20276 reads 2027-03-16 to 2027-03-18 in both. Reading duedate alone as "the event date" would place a three-day show two days late and shorten every lead-time figure by the length of the show.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Not every ticket of this type is a show
rules.value: The summary prefix classifies it: no prefix is a show (261), (COMMUNITY) is a year-long platform engagement (4), (OTHER) is a continuous service such as a webshop (5), (EP LITE) is a light deployment (1).
rules.why: Only a show is a dated deadline. The nine community and engagement records run 364 to 1,099 days, so counting days until one is meaningless. They are shown on the grid and excluded from every countdown and from the next-show figure.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Which client an event belongs to
rules.value: The client token in the labels: everything that is not a four-digit year, not Delivery, not Event and not REGION=. 242 of 275 events carry one, 33 carry none. 55 distinct tokens resolve through the same map the bug labels use, extended with an evidenced alias table.
rules.why: A different mechanism again from bugs (Reported By) and stories (delivery labels), so it is recorded separately. 203 of 275 events resolve to a ledger client. The 33 with no token cannot appear against any client; 20 of them share one identical label set, which looks like a bulk creation that was never tagged.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Event label aliases
rules.value: ADS, ADSGroup and adsgroup.org.uk all mean ADS Group. DWTC and DXBLive both mean Dubai World Trade Centre. MesseFrankfurtUSA, IntlMining, BPL, VDI, VDA, OITE, SNAC, HMP, ISE, K5, NGF and busworld.org each map to their ledger client by name.
rules.why: Three tokens for one client is normal here, so name matching alone is not enough. Every token that does not resolve stays unresolved and appears below rather than being guessed at.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Event tokens that do not resolve
rules.value: premiereeventsbyinforma (8 events) and InformaCosmoprofNA (3) are Informa subsidiaries and need a decision on which entity. CONNECTOman (7) is probably the Connect client but is not evidenced. IEG (5), ROAR (2), BoE, Evoke, SPE, CMPL, AEIB, CIONET are not in the 49-client ledger. SusanTest (4) is test data and is dropped outright. Community, Documentation and EPLite are not client tokens.
rules.why: The bare Informa rule applies here too: the group parent is not a customer, so an Informa-prefixed token is never resolved to it. Resolving these is a data quality task, not a modelling one.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: How an event shows on a grid
rules.value: A cell whose month the event touches gets a rule along its top edge and a diamond in the count line: filled for a show, hollow for a community or engagement record. An event spanning a month boundary marks both months. The cell click lists every event that month with its dates, its distance from today and its Jira status.
rules.why: Drawn in ink rather than a data colour, because an event is an annotation on the time axis and not a series. Giving it a hue would put it in competition with severity, delivery and incidents, which is the collision the colour system exists to prevent.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Next show and the countdown
rules.value: The client's first show whose end date is today or later; the countdown is days from today to its start date
rules.why: Shown on every client row on both grids, amber inside 30 days. A show that has started but not finished reads "event running now" rather than a negative number.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Days between a story and the next show
rules.value: For a story named to a client, the client's first show starting on or after the story landed, and the gap in days
rules.why: Shown on every story analysis card. For a story with no resolution date the placement month is used instead and the card says so, because the gap then inherits the month-basis caveat rather than being a measured date difference.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Shows in 90 days with an Urgent or High bug open
rules.value: Clients with a show starting within 90 days that also have at least one Urgent or High bug open
rules.why: The forward indicator the KPI row carries: 13 of the 18 clients with a show inside 90 days go into it with an Urgent or High still open. It is binary, so the risk matrix on the Timeline tab (rk-*) is the fuller reading: it splits the same book by tier and by window and says which rule fired.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: The workbook and Jira disagree on three events
rules.value: OP-18706 IATF 2027 reads 5 to 11 Nov in Jira and 1 to 5 Nov in the workbook. OP-16585 OSW 2027 and OP-16533 OPES 2027 both read 26 to 28 Apr in Jira against 10 to 14 May and 12 May in the workbook.
rules.why: Jira is treated as the source of truth because it is live and the workbook is a monthly export, but the disagreement is carried on the event row so nobody has to rediscover it. The other 53 events the workbook covers agree exactly.
rules.source: Susan's Customer & Event workbook, August 2026 export

rules.name: One event has its dates the wrong way round
rules.value: OP-12907 Arbeitsschutz 2030 reads start 2030-10-25 and end 2028-10-27
rules.why: A two-year gap with the start after the end, so one of the two is a typo. It is excluded from countdowns and flagged rather than silently reordered.
rules.source: Jira OP project, live through the connector, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Exclude the Hyve dedicated team
rules.why: Hyve Group Plc is the only client on this board with a dedicated team feeding it, so while its HV work is counted Hyve is not like-for-like comparable with the other 48 rows. Set this to 1 to strip every HV item from every view and every headline and get a board where all 49 clients are counted the same way. Default 0 — the work is real and hiding it by default would understate what Hyve is owed.
rules.source: Product decision, 21 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Every view. Hyve's Shipped, In progress, Investment, Open bugs, Severity mix and Liability; the open-client-bugs tile; the timeline, delivery and bugs tabs

rules.name: Count HV open bugs raised before the team formed
rules.why: Three HV bugs are open today but were raised in March 2026, before the dedicated team formed: HV-132 and HV-178 (Medium) and HV-134 (High), all three sitting in Ready for release for six months. The Q2 scope rule excludes them, which is the one place that rule hides something live. Set to 1 to count them and add three bugs, 7 severity points before the age multiplier, to Hyve's liability. Note the EP bug side has no date floor at all — it keeps open bugs back to 2023 in the Pre-2026 column — so 0 here is the inconsistent setting, chosen deliberately to match the scope decision.
rules.source: Product decision, 21 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Hyve's open bug count, severity mix and liability; the open-client-bugs tile; the timeline's Pre-2026 and March columns

rules.name: HV is a team, not a project
rules.value: Call it the Hyve dedicated team. Never 'the HV project' in anything a reader sees.
rules.why: It is a dedicated team standing up work for one client under its own EM and PO, formed after Q1 2026. Naming it a project invites the reader to compare it with EP, which is a platform serving 49 clients.
rules.source: Ajay, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Attribution is project membership
rules.value: Every Story and Bug in HV belongs to Hyve Group Plc, Pipedrive 4121. No label lookup, no Reported-by read, no Pipedrive field read.
rules.why: The normal route would find almost nothing: only 3 of 175 HV items carry a Hyve label and only 8 carry a Pipedrive Company ID. Membership of the project is the attribution, and it is exact.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Which client every HV item lands on

rules.name: The INTERNAL discard does not apply to HV
rules.value: On the EP side a ticket whose every Reported-by value is INTERNAL is discarded as not a client experience. In HV that rule is switched off.
rules.why: 36 of 175 HV items carry Reported by = INTERNAL. Applying the EP rule would delete a fifth of the team's work from a board whose whole point is showing what that team built for this client.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Scope: Story and Bug at hierarchy level 0
rules.value: issuetype in (Story, Bug), created >= 2026-04-01. 153 of the project's 517 issues.
rules.why: One ticket, one distinct deliverable. Level 0 is what a client experiences; anything below it is how the work was cut up.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Everything HV contributes

rules.name: What is deliberately out of scope
rules.value: Sub-task (166) and Defect (95) are hierarchy level -1 and never counted. Task (55), Feature Request (2) and Epic (24) are out too.
rules.why: Defect is an in-sprint development bug raised against work in flight, not something a client hit — counting it would double-count the story it hangs off and inflate the bug figure by 95. Task and Feature Request were left out pending a look at what they actually hold.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Three-stage delivery model
rules.value: To Do: Open, Ready to start. In Delivery: In Progress, In testing, Ready for testing, Ready for UAT, Ready for release. Delivered: Done. Every HV status in use maps; none is unaccounted for.
rules.why: Collapsing the intermediate stages gives an honest WIP count. Ready for release alone holds 21 of the 37 items in flight, so most of what is 'in delivery' is in fact staged and waiting, which a single In Progress bucket would hide.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Rejected is a STATUS, not a resolution
rules.value: Delivered means status = Done. It does NOT mean statusCategory = Done, and the clause resolution != Rejected does not filter Rejected work.
rules.why: This is the correction that matters. 30 of the 95 HV Story and Bug items in the Done category sit in status Rejected. resolution = Rejected returns zero issues, so the published board query statusCategory = Done AND resolution != Rejected returns 77 against a true 65 — it keeps 18 Rejected tickets that happen to carry some other resolution and silently drops 6 genuinely delivered ones whose resolution is empty, because Jira's != also excludes nulls. Overstated by 18 percent. On a 30-day window it reads 24 against a true 18.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Every delivered figure. Also a live error on the HV board today

rules.name: What counts as delivered
rules.value: Story with status Done. In scope that is 32 shipped, 22 in delivery, 29 in the backlog and 11 rejected.
rules.why: Backlog items are not delivery and do not enter investment. Rejected items are counted nowhere at all: not as delivered, not as in flight, not as liability.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: HV bugs are liability, never delivery
rules.value: An open HV bug joins Hyve's liability and the lower timeline strip exactly like an EP client bug. A closed HV bug counts nowhere: 26 fixed bugs in scope appear on no figure here.
rules.why: This keeps Hyve comparable with the other 48 clients on both axes, because that is precisely how EP bugs already work: open bugs are liability, bug fixes are not counted as investment. The cost is that the team's bug-fixing throughput is invisible on this board. That number belongs on the HV delivery board, not here.
rules.source: Product decision, 21 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Hyve's liability, severity mix and open bug count

rules.name: Scope starts at Q2 2026
rules.value: created >= 2026-04-01, when the dedicated team formed. 22 earlier items are excluded, 10 of them from 2025.
rules.why: Before Q2 the work ran under a different operating model, so mixing it in would describe a team that did not exist. The one thing this hides is three bugs that are open today — see the pre-Q2 rule above, which can put them back.
rules.source: Ajay, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Hyve is not like-for-like while HV is counted
rules.value: With HV counted, Hyve is the largest row on this board on both axes. Investment goes from 21 to 75 against IMEX at 17; liability goes from 12 to 67.8 against Frankfurter Buchmesse at 66.5 (measured 22 Sep 2026 with the default rules).
rules.why: Nothing about Hyve changed. One client acquired a dedicated team whose tickets are visible while nobody else's are, so Hyve tops both axes for a reason that has nothing to do with how it is being served. Read the ranking with that in mind, or switch the exclude rule on.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026
rules.drives: How every ranking, the quadrant and the Neglected tile should be read

rules.name: HV stories are not part of the 650
rules.value: The Stories in 2026 tile, the named-versus-platform split and the 91 percent banner all count the 650 EP stories only. HV items are shown as a separate addition.
rules.why: The 650 is a documented, AI-enriched population built by the Delivery Timeline generator under its own scope rule. HV is a different population built a different way. Adding them into one number would make both unreproducible.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026
rules.drives: The stories tile, the ledger banner, the named and platform split

rules.name: HV items are carried unenriched
rules.value: No AI summary, problem, why, outcome, theme, product area, business value or confidence rating. The Jira summary is shown as written, and the theme reads 'not theme-classified'.
rules.why: The Delivery Timeline generator has never run over HV. Rather than leave the fields blank and let a reader assume the classification is missing by accident, every HV card says so.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: Delivery mix runs 59 to 41, not 70 to 30
rules.value: 103 Stories against 72 Bugs across the whole project. The standard board baseline of 70-80 percent stories does not hold here.
rules.why: Not necessarily wrong for a dedicated team absorbing a single client's production load, but a board scored against the standard baseline will read as a permanent fail. Either set a different target for this team or stop scoring it against that one.
rules.source: Checked live against the HV project, 21 Sep 2026

rules.name: The pipeline ledger is the source of truth
rules.value: Rows and the column schema live in this artifact's shared database. The Confluence page is a snapshot of 18 Sep 2026 and now points here. Schema 2 (22 Sep 2026) added Team, Driver and Rationale and cut Why to one line. Since 22 Sep 2026 every change is recorded with who made it and when (pp-history).
rules.why: Two editable copies of a commitment list drift within days. One place, edited in the open, with every change visible to everyone who can open the page.
rules.source: Product decision, 22 Sep 2026
rules.drives: The whole Pipeline tab

rules.name: What earns a row
rules.value: A committed customer obligation; a compliance, security, legal or regulatory requirement; something preventing significant revenue, retention, operational or reputational risk; a committed launch or strategic priority; or an unblocker for one of those. One row per feature per target month.
rules.why: Without a bar, a must-have list becomes a wish list and stops meaning anything when resources are argued over.
rules.source: Definition of Must-Have, Confluence page 2155872263

rules.name: Month, Area and Status are normalised; the original wording is kept
rules.value: Month becomes YYYY-MM, Area and Status collapse to one spelling each. Whatever the owner originally wrote is kept on the item and shown in its form.
rules.why: The source had four spellings of two months and three of one product area, which is exactly what stops a ledger being totalled. Discarding the original wording would lose real meaning — 'In progress (targeting 30 Sep)' says more than 'In Progress'.
rules.source: Imported from Confluence page 2155872263, 22 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Every roll-up, filter and group

rules.name: How an estimate becomes person-days
rules.value: A 'Total: N person-days' line wins. Otherwise a range like 15-20d takes the midpoint and is badged mid. Otherwise every Nd figure in the cell is summed. A cell mentioning pending, required or rough is badged partial. Anything else counts as no estimate.
rules.why: Owners write estimates four different ways. Parsing them is the only route to an effort total, and each rule is shown on the row so a reader can see which one fired rather than trusting a number.
rules.source: Imported from Confluence page 2155872263, 22 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Committed effort, all three roll-ups, group subtotals

rules.name: Unestimated items count as zero and are named
rules.value: An item with no parseable estimate contributes nothing to any total, and the count of such items sits next to every total that they affect.
rules.why: The alternative is a total that silently understates. A month reading 89 days across 11 items where 4 carry no estimate is not a 89-day month, and the ledger has to say so.
rules.source: Imported from Confluence page 2155872263, 22 Sep 2026

rules.name: Jira columns are read-only
rules.value: Jira status, due date, logged time and the flags come from the ticket and cannot be typed into. They are refreshed when someone asks Claude to refresh them, and the refresh date is shown.
rules.why: A stated status is an intent and a Jira status is a fact. Keeping both, and marking which is which, is what makes drift visible instead of arguable.
rules.source: Imported from Confluence page 2155872263, 22 Sep 2026
rules.drives: The drift, overdue, due-soon and over-estimate flags

rules.name: Drift is stated status against Jira status
rules.value: Both are mapped to the same eight-state vocabulary and compared. A mismatch badges the row and adds it to the drift alert.
rules.why: The imported page was four days old and six rows had already moved. Drift is the cheapest signal that a commitment list has stopped describing reality.
rules.source: Imported from Confluence page 2155872263, 22 Sep 2026

rules.name: Columns are editable and shared
rules.value: Any column can be renamed, retyped, reordered or removed from the column menu in its header, and hidden from your own table. Renames, moves, additions and removals are written to the shared schema, so they apply for everyone, and each is recorded in History and can be undone. Hiding is per viewer. The columns the grid, the totals and the form depend on (Feature, Month, Status, Driver, Team, Jira, Estimate) can be hidden but not removed. Removing a column stops it being shown; the values already typed into it stay in the database.
rules.why: A source of truth nobody can reshape gets abandoned for a spreadsheet. Keeping removed values means a column removed in haste comes back, values and all, with Undo.
rules.source: Product decision, 22 Sep 2026

rules.name: First risk window
rules.why: A bug's severity is not fixed: proximity to the client's next show is a multiplier. A Medium 90 days out is a backlog item; the same Medium five days out is an incident that has not happened yet. The first column holds clients whose next show starts within this many days.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.3
rules.drives: Risk matrix on the Timeline tab, the Exposure column on the ledger

rules.name: Second risk window
rules.why: The second column: next show after the first window and within this many days. Must sit above the first window and below the third.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.3
rules.drives: Risk matrix on the Timeline tab, the Exposure column on the ledger

rules.name: Third risk window
rules.why: The third column. Beyond it, and for a client with no dated show at all, the client sits in the none column.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.3
rules.drives: Risk matrix on the Timeline tab, the Exposure column on the ledger

rules.name: The window comes from the client's next show, not the bug's event
rules.value: Client-level: days from the snapshot date to the start of the client's next dated show (ev-next-show). The event a bug names (its ev field) is not used.
rules.why: Bug-level event attribution exists on some rows but not reliably; client-level is complete. Recorded as a known limitation, not hidden.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.3

rules.name: Clients with no dated show get their own column and an always-on rule
rules.value: The none column holds clients whose next show is beyond the third window, and clients with no dated show at all. The ones with no dated show have no countdown, so the always-on rule (rk-always-on-days) reads them instead.
rules.why: 9 of the 271 event records are (COMMUNITY), (OTHER) or (EP LITE): year-round engagements running 364 to 1,099 days, where a countdown is meaningless. Without the always-on rule a continuous-service client silently drops out of the risk view.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.3

rules.name: Untiered clients get their own row
rules.value: Tier 1, Tier 2, Tier 3, Tier 4, then No tier. Every client sits in exactly one row, and the matrix states the count so the check can be read off the page.
rules.why: K5 GmbH is in Jira and the contract sheet but no longer Phase = Active, so it carries no tier. It must not vanish.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.4

rules.name: Tier is reported, never blended into a score
rules.value: Tier and window stay two axes. No figure on the page multiplies or adds them together.
rules.why: Two Urgents on a Tier 1 client at 20 days and the same on a Tier 4 client are different situations. A blended score would rank them by an exchange rate nobody agreed.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.2, principle 4

rules.name: Open stories are not counted as risk
rules.value: Counted: open client bugs by severity, non-cancelled incidents, must-haves committed to land after the client's show. Not counted: open stories, closed bugs, cancelled incidents.
rules.why: An open story is work in flight, not a risk. Counting it inverts the signal: a client with twenty stories in flight would rank worse than a client with none, when the client with none is the neglected one. The delivery-side risk signal is the broken-promise rule and nothing else.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.5

rules.name: Red: Urgent open, Tier 1-2, show within N days
rules.why: Any Urgent open on a Tier 1 or Tier 2 client whose next show starts within this many days turns the client red. Invented here; no upstream authority computes it, so it will need arguing exactly as the severity weights did.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.6
rules.drives: Red flags in the risk matrix and the Exposure column

rules.name: Red: any High open with a show within N days
rules.why: Any High open on any client, any tier, whose next show starts within this many days turns the client red. Spec §1.6 names it rk-high-14.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.6
rules.drives: Red flags in the risk matrix and the Exposure column

rules.name: Amber: bug older than N days with a show inside the second window
rules.why: An open bug raised more than this many days ago, on a client whose next show starts inside the second window (rk-window-60), turns the client amber: it is not getting fixed by accident. Spec §1.6 names it rk-ageing.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.6
rules.drives: Amber flags in the risk matrix and the Exposure column

rules.name: Red: a must-have committed to land after the client's show
rules.value:
broken := the pipeline item's Driver is a client
       AND the item is not Done
       AND the last day of the item's month falls after that client's next show starts
rules.why: The sharpest flag here, and binary rather than weighted: an item sitting in October for a client whose show is in September is a broken commitment before anyone reads a number, and the client has already been told. Red at any tier. It can only fire on items with a Driver, so the count of items without one is printed next to it rather than read as zero.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.7. Added in build: §1.6 names the rule, §7.1 did not list it
rules.drives: Risk matrix on the Timeline tab, the Exposure column on the ledger, the month x team grid

rules.name: Amber: no dated show, and a High open more than N days
rules.why: A client with no dated show gets no countdown, so this reads it instead: any Urgent open, or any High open longer than this many days, turns it amber. Spec §1.6 names it rk-always-on; §7.1 did not list it, so its threshold had no home.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §1.6. Added in build
rules.drives: Amber flags for clients with no dated show

rules.name: Investment and liability are never netted
rules.value: Investment and liability sit side by side in the ledger and on the two axes of the quadrant. No figure subtracts one from the other, and the word balance is retired.
rules.why: Custom build is chosen: someone decided to spend those days. A bug is incurred: nobody chose it. A client with heavy delivery and heavy bugs is not balanced; they are getting a lot of attention and a lot of breakage, which is a third story a single line cannot express.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §4.1

rules.name: The two axes have incomparable coverage
rules.value: Bugs attribute to a client almost completely. Stories attribute at 61 of 650.
rules.why: One axis is near-complete and the other is 9% complete. A shared chart implies a parity that does not exist, so each axis states its own coverage.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §4.1

rules.name: Investment is counts, not days, in v1
rules.value: What we chose to spend on this client: 2026 stories carrying the client's Jira label, shipped or in progress, plus pipeline items whose Driver is the client. A pipeline item whose ticket is already one of those stories is counted once.
rules.why: Estimate coverage is 193 of 1,201 stories, so a person-days axis cannot be fed (decision D1).
rules.source: Decision D1, Ajay, 22 Sep 2026. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §4.2

rules.name: Liability = severity x age multiplier + incident points
rules.value:
liability := sum over open bugs of severity_weight x age_multiplier
           + incident_points x non-cancelled incidents
rules.why: The old pain figure treated a 400-day-old open bug and a 4-day-old one identically. The shape matters more than the values: a bug open for a year is a worse liability than the same bug raised last week. Severity weights are the sev-* rules; points per incident is incident-points; age is days from creation to the snapshot date.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §4.3
rules.drives: Liability column, the quadrant, the Neglected tile

rules.name: Age multiplier, 0-30 days
rules.why: An open bug raised in the last 30 days counts at its plain severity weight.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §4.3
rules.drives: Liability column, the quadrant, the Neglected tile

rules.name: Age multiplier, 31-90 days
rules.why: A bug that has survived a month is starting to look structural.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §4.3
rules.drives: Liability column, the quadrant, the Neglected tile

rules.name: Age multiplier, 91-180 days
rules.why: A quarter or more open. The same boundary where the Client Bug Score half-life bites.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §4.3
rules.drives: Liability column, the quadrant, the Neglected tile

rules.name: Age multiplier, over 180 days
rules.why: 29 of the 84 EP open bugs were raised before January 2026; the oldest is from September 2023. A year-old open bug is a worse liability than the same bug raised last week.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §4.3
rules.drives: Liability column, the quadrant, the Neglected tile

rules.name: Quadrant thresholds are the running median, not fixed
rules.value: High investment and high liability each mean above the median across the Planhat-Active clients, recomputed from the stored data every time the page draws. Healthy partner: high investment, low liability. Expensive and still broken: high on both. Quiet: low on both. Neglected: high liability, low investment.
rules.why: So nobody reads the lines as absolutes. With most clients carrying no named delivery the investment median is 0, so high investment means at least one item. The two dangerous cells share the high-liability side, one above the other, and need completely different conversations: one is getting a lot of attention and still breaking, the other is breaking and getting none.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §4.4

rules.name: Retired 22 Sep 2026: pain, give, balance and the give-and-get chart
rules.value:
pain-formula: sum(severity weight of each open bug) + points-per-incident x non-cancelled incidents
