give-formula: count of 2026 stories carrying that client's Jira label; shipped and in-progress counted separately
top-balance: 14 clients in the give-and-get chart
balState: no activity / nothing open / no named delivery / N shipped vs N open
Pain, no named delivery (KPI): pain above 0, nothing shipped or in progress
rules.why: Replaced by investment, liability and exposure (spec v1 §4; decision O2, replace rather than keep both). Two charts answering the same question in contradictory ways is worse than either alone. The formulas stay here verbatim so an old figure can still be reconstructed.
rules.source: Decision O2, Ajay, 22 Sep 2026. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §4.5

rules.name: The flow clock starts at first entry to In progress
rules.value: Everything earlier is backlog (D2): Awaiting Estimation, Estimated request, Tech Brief, Brief ready for review, Ready for decomposition, Ready for development, Open, Ready to start and PM Review. Backlog time after the clock has started is excluded too.
rules.why: Consequence: total flow is NOT time-to-customer. On both tickets the spec sampled, the largest single delay sat in Awaiting Estimation, before this clock starts; across the flow sample the median ticket waited 3.9 days between creation and first In progress. Any figure from the Flow tab quoted against a show date must be read that way, and the tab labels it so.
rules.source: Decision D2, Ajay, 22 Sep 2026. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §5.3

rules.name: Build and handoff is one number, not dev time and QA queue
rules.value: Build and handoff runs from the first entry to In progress to the first entry to In testing: dev, review, the review queue and the QA queue together.
rules.why: The deciding rule. On EP-57014 the developer never moved the ticket out of In progress; the QA made both transitions two seconds apart, so In progress silently absorbed the whole handoff. In the flow sample 22 of the 46 measured QA cycles lasted under 15 minutes: the ticket was moved through In testing after the testing was done. Publishing a split would publish a number known to be wrong.
rules.source: Decision D3, Ajay, 22 Sep 2026. Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §5.2

rules.name: The three measured intervals and their boundaries
rules.value:
Build and handoff: In progress, Code review and merge, Ready for review, In review, Ready for testing.
QA cycle: In testing (Task in testing before 15 Sep).
Release hold: Ready for release; before 15 Sep also QA Tested, Ready for deploy, Staged for Release, RC approved, Direct Deploy, Merged to Master/Mobile env.
Total flow: the three summed. On-hold keeps the interval it interrupted.
rules.why: Every state belongs to exactly one interval, so the three always sum to the total and a loop back to In progress re-enters build time instead of vanishing. On a first pass the boundaries read In progress, then In testing, then Ready for release, then Done. No hotfix path is split out (D4).
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §5.3; decision D4, Ajay, 22 Sep 2026

rules.name: Time in a state sums across every visit
rules.value: Time in a state is summed across every visit, not taken from the first. Done is the last move into Done; time spent Done before a reopen is excluded.
rules.why: A regression loop re-enters In progress; taking the first visit understates it. The incident method documents the same trap: IMP-321 went Testing, Done, Testing, Done, and taking the first done transition understated MTTR by a day.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §5.4

rules.name: Parent-level intervals are correct for split stories
rules.value: Intervals are read at parent level. For a split story the parent sits In progress while sub-tasks do the work, which is the true elapsed build window.
rules.why: No sub-task roll-up in v1. Defects and Sub-tasks are never rows of their own; they are read as children of their parent.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §5.3 and §5.9

rules.name: QA cycle contains defect-fix time and is not called QA time
rules.value: The story stays In testing while its Defects are fixed, so the QA cycle is testing plus fixing.
rules.why: Calling it QA time would charge QA with developer rework.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §5.3 and §5.5

rules.name: Defect sub-task count is the rework volume signal
rules.value: The Defect sub-tasks under an item. Volume: QA found N problems. The primary quality signal.
rules.why: A count, not an inferred loop, and it names the developer. EP-57014 carries two live Defects (EP-57602, EP-57658). In the flow sample 55 Defects sit under 8 items.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §5.5

rules.name: The four loop types are reported separately, never summed
rules.value:
Rework: In review to In progress. Caught at review; cheap and healthy.
Send back: In testing to In progress. Rare by design, because the normal path is a Defect.
Regression failed: Ready for release to In progress. Passed QA and still broke; the release window restarts.
Reopened: Done back into the chain. Escaped to production.
rules.why: Five Defects and no send-back is QA doing its job; one send-back is something else. They read completely differently and must not be summed into a rework score.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §5.5

rules.name: Strip weekends from every flow figure
rules.why: A story entering In progress at 17:00 on a Friday and worked on Monday would otherwise show three days of build, none of it work: a 60% error on a five-day story. Weekends are stripped in UTC. flow.json stores both, so switching this recomputes nothing.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §5.8
rules.drives: Every duration on the Flow tab

rules.name: Public holidays are not stripped
rules.value: Weekends only.
rules.why: The teams span Kyiv, Warsaw, Helsinki and Calcutta with four different calendars, and four holiday tables is more machinery than the accuracy is worth. Recorded as a known overstatement rather than silently absorbed.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §5.8

rules.name: Every EP status maps to exactly one interval
rules.value:
backlog: Awaiting Estimation, Estimated request, Tech Brief, Brief ready for review, Ready for decomposition, Ready for development, Open, Ready to start, PM Review
build: In progress, Code review and merge, Ready for review, In review, Ready for testing
qa: In testing, Task in testing
release: Ready for release, QA Tested, Ready for deploy, Staged for Release, RC approved, Direct Deploy, Merged to Master/Mobile env
pause: On-hold (keeps the interval it interrupted)
done: Done, COMPLETE
rejected: Rejected, Closed by reject (out of scope)
rules.why: A status mapped to nothing is time lost silently, so the unmapped-states check must return zero before a rebuild ships. The map covers both workflow generations, because the 15 Sep 2026 migration renamed several states. A new EP status must be added here before the next pull.
rules.source: Read from the changelogs of the flow sample, 22 Sep 2026. Added in build

rules.name: The 15 Sep 2026 workflow migration
rules.value: Between 16:45 and 16:55 UTC on 15 Sep 2026 every open EP ticket was bulk-moved to the new workflow: COMPLETE became DONE; RC approved, Staged for Release, QA Tested and Direct Deploy moved to Ready for release; Ready for deploy was renamed QA Tested.
rules.why: A loop inside that window is the migration, not rework, and is never counted. 24 of the sampled rows crossed it inside their release hold; their time is kept, because the migration only relabelled the state.
rules.source: Read from the changelogs of the flow sample, 22 Sep 2026. Added in build

rules.name: A months-old release state closed in the clean-up is not a release hold
rules.value: A done row that sat more than 20 business days in one pre-migration release state, until the migration moved it, is flagged and left out of the release-hold and total medians. It stays on the Flow tab with its flag.
rules.why: EP-48822 sat 223 days in RC approved and was closed the day after the migration: its release hold reads the clean-up, not the release train. 4 sampled rows match. Principle: a number known to be wrong is not published, and the rows it drops are counted.
rules.source: Read from the changelogs of the flow sample, 22 Sep 2026. Added in build

rules.name: A loop that comes back within N minutes is a click-through
rules.why: Moving a ticket back and forth within minutes is a correction, not rework. Loops faster than this are kept on the row, with their timing, but not counted on the ladder. The ladder is recounted from the stored loop events, so changing this needs no new pull.
rules.source: Invented by this dashboard. Added in build
rules.drives: The rework ladder on the Flow tab

rules.name: The flow figures are a sample until the batch runs
rules.value: 50 EP stories and bugs that reached Done between 2 Sep 2026 and 22 Sep 2026 (35 stories, 15 bugs), plus the 15 pipeline tickets in scope so the queue picture carries work in flight. Picked as the most recently finished work, so it over-represents the fortnight around the 15 Sep workflow migration. The full scope is about 1,200 EP stories and bugs created in 2026; the full pull is a scheduled batch, not a chat session.
rules.why: Two tickets is not a sample (spec §10); 64 is enough to see the shape and too few to quote a median to a client. The page reads whatever flow.json holds and says which it is, so the batch replaces the sample without a rebuild.
rules.source: Pulled through the Atlassian connector, 22 Sep 2026. Added in build

rules.name: Team is the ledger's unit; the person is Raised by and enters no total
rules.value: Owner is relabelled Raised by. It stays on the row and appears in no roll-up; effort rolls up by team only.
rules.why: Kavi is a PO; he is not doing 58 days of work. The owner roll-up measured who filled in the form, not who does the work.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §2
rules.drives: Effort by team, the Team filter and grouping

rules.name: Team comes from the Jira ticket, else it is a required field
rules.value:
1. The row has a Jira key and the ticket carries a team (customfield_10001): that team.
2. Otherwise the row's own Team field.
3. Neither: badged no team, left out of the team roll-ups and counted in the unassigned line beneath them.
rules.why: One PO spans several teams: Alex's items cross Global Search, Sessions and Networking, so a person-to-team map would not hold. Two rows sit in rule 3 on 22 Sep 2026: the Iyzico migration has no ticket, and EP-57297 is an epic whose ticket carries no team.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §2.2
rules.drives: The Team column, Effort by team, the month x team grid

rules.name: Driver is a named client or Platform; Tier derives from it
rules.value: Driver: a client from the Planhat active list, or Platform. Tier: that client's Sales Tier; blank for Platform. Driver is distinct from Priority: Priority says why it is a must-have, Driver says who it is for.
rules.why: Many must-haves have no client; re-architecting session search is platform work. Forcing it into a tier band would be a lie with a colour on it. Driver unlocks the tier on a row, promise-versus-show, the event overlay and investment per client.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §3.4 and §3.5
rules.drives: Tier, the broken-promise rule, the event overlay, investment

rules.name: Why is one line with a hard limit; long prose moves to Rationale
rules.why: A field that is sometimes a sentence and sometimes an essay cannot be read in a table. The editor enforces the limit. On migration the old text moved to Rationale verbatim and Why started empty, so nothing was lost and nobody's wording was truncated by a machine.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §3.3
rules.drives: The Why editor on the Pipeline tab and its over-limit badge

rules.name: Driver was pre-filled only where the row names a client
rules.value: 22 Sep 2026: DLG Markets GmbH (Pipedrive 81808) on the five rows whose Why read "DLG commitment"; IMEX (26874) on EP-57221 ("Critical for IMEX") and EP-57297 (Impact: "Currently a major blocker for IMEX."). The other eleven rows were left blank and badged Driver not set.
rules.why: A driver guessed from a PO's name or a product area would put a tier on a commitment nobody made. The quoted text is stored on each pre-filled row and shown in its form.
rules.source: Product decision, Ajay, 22 Sep 2026. Added in build

rules.name: The month x team grid runs on the pipeline's own months
rules.value: Columns are the months the pipeline commits to (Sep 2026 to Jan 2027). Rows are teams, banded by Driver: one band per client with its show dates drawn on the same axis, then Platform, then Driver not set. A cell lists its items as cards, under their count and day total; click a card to open the item, or + Add to add one there.
rules.why: The spec asked for the Delivery grid's month set so the two read alike. Those months are all past and the pipeline is all future, so the same set would draw an empty grid; the shape, cells and banding are kept instead.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §3.1 and §3.2. Added in build

rules.name: Overload is an arithmetic fact, not a capacity model
rules.value: A team's committed person-days in a month are compared with the weekdays in that month. Above it, the team's cells for that month are marked over.
rules.why: It says only that the committed days are more than one person could work in that month. Team size and availability are not recorded, so it is not a capacity calculation and must not be read as one.
rules.source: Spec v1, Risk, Flow and Investment, 22 Sep 2026 §3.1. Added in build

rules.name: Computed once, stored as JSON, never re-pulled on page load
rules.value:
LEDGER and HYVE, inline JSON in the page: the Jira, Planhat, Drive and OP pulls.
logic.json: this registry.
The shared database: the pipeline ledger and its column schema.
flow.json: the changelog read, every transition and per-state duration, and the summary the Flow tab draws.
rules.why: The changelog read is one call per issue and takes minutes; it must not run on every view. The page only does arithmetic over stored values and live rules, so a changed rule recomputes instantly and a refresh is a deliberate step with a date on it.
rules.source: Product decision, Ajay, 22 Sep 2026. Added in build

rules.name: Every 2026 story is cached with its what, why and outcome, and later runs pull only the delta
rules.value: Scope: project = EP AND issuetype = Story AND created >= 2026-01-01 AND status != Rejected (1,192 on 24 Sep 2026). One record per story in data/stories/cache/stories.json: Jira fields, epic, and an ai block (summary, problem, why, outcome, theme, product area, business value, run/grow/transform, impact, confidence). The 650 page stories keep their inherited text; the other 546 were written on 24 Sep to data/stories/SPEC.md. A later run reads keys and updated dates for the whole scope, re-reads only stories whose updated moved, fetches descriptions and rewrites the ai block only for new stories or ones whose summary or description changed, and marks a story that leaves the scope rather than deleting it.
rules.why: Enriching 1,192 stories costs hours of reads and writing; a refresh should cost only what changed. It also documents the generator for the first time (runbook Source 3).
rules.source: Ajay, 24 Sep 2026. The cache is not yet on the page: the page still reports on the 650 until the 650-versus-1,192 decision is taken.

rules.name: Every change to the pipeline is recorded, and can be undone
rules.value: Each add, field change, removal and restore is written into the item itself, in the same database write as the change: who made it (their user id, shown to each viewer as a name), when (UTC), which field, and the value before and after. Fields saved together form one entry. Removing an item hides it and keeps it, with its history, under Removed, where it can be restored; nothing on the page deletes a row. Column changes are recorded on the column schema the same way. Claude's import from Confluence and the schema-2 migration are recorded as Claude; changes made before this version went live on 22 Sep 2026 were not recorded one by one.
rules.why: The ledger is the source of truth for what we promised clients, and a promise that changed silently is worse than no ledger. Keeping the record on the item means it cannot drift away from the item, and writing both in one update means a change can never land without its record.
rules.source: Comment on the artifact from the owner, 22 Sep 2026: "history of changes must be tracked"
rules.drives: History panel, the history in the item form, Undo and Revert, Removed and Restore

rules.name: The Pipeline tab opens on the Month x team grid
rules.value: The grid is the default view and the table is one click away. A viewer's choice of view, grouping and hidden columns is remembered in their own browser only; it changes nothing for anyone else.
rules.why: The first question the pipeline answers is what each team has committed to in each month. The table is for scanning and quick edits.
rules.source: Comment on the artifact from the owner, 22 Sep 2026: "Month X team should be the default"
rules.drives: Pipeline tab

rules.name: Items are added and changed in one form, and nothing is saved until Save
rules.value: The item form shows every column, labelled, with the two required fields marked: Feature and Month. Why is one line with a live counter; Team is only asked for when the Jira ticket carries none; Driver lists Platform and the Planhat active clients by tier; the estimate is read back as the days it will count; a Jira key is checked for shape. + Add in a grid cell opens the form with that cell's month, team and driver filled in. Save writes only the fields that changed. Every save can be undone from the notice that follows it, from the item's history or from the History panel. A table cell can still be changed in place, and is recorded the same way.
rules.why: The old Add button wrote a blank row the moment it was pressed, and editing was an invisible click-to-edit: two blank rows were left behind on 22 Sep. A form with an explicit Save makes adding and changing deliberate, and shows what will be saved before it is.
rules.source: Comment on the artifact from the owner, 22 Sep 2026: "editing / updating / adding is not clear super hard"
rules.drives: + New item, + Add on the grid, Open in the table, the item form

rules.name: An item with no Feature is a draft and counts nowhere
rules.value: A row whose Feature is empty sits outside every total, the grid, the risk matrix and the investment figures. It is listed above the grid, to be finished or removed. The form will not save an item without a Feature, so drafts can only come from before 22 Sep 2026.
rules.why: A blank row is not a commitment. Counting it inflated the item count and would have put empty cards on the grid.
rules.source: Invented here, 22 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Pipeline counts, the grid, the drafts strip

rules.name: Every save of this registry is logged inside logic.json
rules.value: A save appends who saved (user id), when, the new version, and every rule added, changed or removed with its old and new value, to the log in logic.json. The last 200 saves are kept. History of saves on the Logic tab lists them, newest first.
rules.why: These rules drive every number on the page. A weight that moved without a record cannot be explained later, and the log travels with the artifact wherever it is copied.
rules.source: Comment on the artifact from the owner, 22 Sep 2026: "history of changes must be tracked"
rules.drives: Logic tab: History of saves

rules.name: The page never relies on the browser's confirm, prompt or alert
rules.value: Every question is asked in a dialog drawn by the page, and every result in a notice at the foot of the screen, with Undo where it applies.
rules.why: An artifact runs in a sandboxed frame, and a sandbox can suppress those browser dialogs, which turns Remove, Import or Add column into a silent no-op.
rules.source: Invented here, 22 Sep 2026
rules.drives: Every question and notice on the page

method.title: How bugs move the Health Score

blocks.text: Live in production, reviewed 14 Sep 2026. Score runs 0 to 10 and starts at 5.0. Recomputed nightly at 01:10 UTC by n8n from Jira EP, Hyve and IMP, written to four Planhat company fields.

Together the three factors can remove at most -3.5. Anything raised before the client's most recent Won deal counts at 25%. Formula must stay linear, not linear (bounded), or the worst accounts score clean.
The signal is "Reported by", not "Affected clients". Resolution order:
Every Reported-by value INTERNAL: discard, not a client experience.
A label with an override mapping: use those companies only.
Otherwise Planhat's own companyIds on the synced Issue.
Otherwise map each label through the Reported-by Label Dictionary to a Pipedrive company id, then to the Planhat company.
A ticket with several Reported-by values counts in full against every one of them, so one platform bug penalises ten accounts identically. If several accounts move together, check that first.
Which client gets the story
New here, and much weaker than the bug side:
A story counts for a client only if Jira names that client on it, in its Reported by field. 70 of 684 stories do.

Labels are joined to Planhat companies through the same Pipedrive id dictionary the bug side uses, learned from how Bug Radar already resolved those labels. A3, Farnborough and Cosmoprof had no bug-side precedent and were mapped by name.
INTERNAL-labelled and unlabelled stories become the platform band. They are never attributed to a client, and never counted in a client's Shipped column.
So "0 shipped" means nothing was recorded against their name, not that nothing reached them. Treat the Investment column as a question to ask, not an answer — and never net it against liability.
Operational traps
Planhat returns HTTP 200 for a field name that does not exist. Renaming any of the four fields in Planhat silently freezes every company on yesterday's value.
Closure is detected from the status name, not statusCategory. A new "closed" status that matches none of the known substrings keeps its bugs counted as open.
Caps and weights live in three places: the Planhat Health Score Profile, the n8n Compute Health Factors node, and the Weekly Digest QUALITY array.
Story summaries are AI-written from the Jira description and any linked spec. 97 of 684 are flagged low confidence and marked as such wherever they appear.

A client-side merge of two existing dashboards — the Client Bug Radar (17 Sep) and the Delivery Timeline (16 Sep). Both originals are untouched; this page holds a copy of their data and reorganises it around the client rather than the team. Jira, Confluence, the workbook and Planhat all pull through connectors; only the 2026 story feed is still re-inherited by hand. The pipeline ledger lives in this artifact’s shared database, the logic registry in logic.json and the flow extract in flow.json: every pull is stored once and read, never re-run on page load.

The Flow tab is parked since 26 Sep 2026. Its logic, the sample it read and how to bring it back are kept in exploration/flow.md; the one-line flow summary on a sampled story card still reads flow.json.

Every 4 hours at most, the page asks Jira for EP bugs and stories changed since the last refresh, through the Atlassian connector of whoever has the page open. The changes go into this artifact's shared database, so everyone sees them, and are laid over the built data: closed bugs drop out, new client bugs appear, stories that shipped move. Only one viewer refreshes at a time. New stories keep Jira's own summary until the next rebuild adds the analysis. Planhat health scores and incidents still update at rebuild.

18 must-have items held in this artifact’s shared database, schema 2 since 22 Sep 2026: Team from the Jira ticket, Driver (who it is for), a one-line Why with the old text kept as Rationale. Jira status, due date and logged time are read per row and dated.
